items.findings: Both quotations verified verbatim in the cached Foresight copies (paper: 'Overview: the spectre', first sentence; abstract page: second paragraph and opening line). Sense meets the criterion. Two problems. (1) Policy: 'Earliest located texts' says the attested date decides which text is earliest located and 'a text known only from an undated later copy cannot be'. The Foresight copy carries no date of its own (attested: null); 1997 rests on its self-description as a draft for the Fifth Foresight Conference and on Goertzel's 2011 report of an unnamed '1997 article'. As recorded, the earliest-located role conflicts with the policy rule. (2) The statement's sense ('AI systems that might rival or surpass the human brain') is not shown by either quoted passage; it comes from an unquoted sentence in section 'Artificial intelligence as a factor': 'By advanced artificial general intelligence, I mean AI systems that rival or surpass the human brain in complexity and speed, that can acquire, manipulate and reason with general knowledge...'. Also 'might' is the pack's softening; the text defines the term without a modal. Independent quick check: Crossref query.bibliographic "artificial general intelligence" to 1997-12-31 (200 rows) found no title with the phrase. Archive lookup for a 1998-2000 capture failed again (429 / connection reset).
items.proposedFix: Either obtain a dated archive capture (or another dated copy, e.g. a 1998 proceedings/reprint) and fill 'attested', or mark the role as provisional per policy (earliest located only on claimed date; show 'claimed 1997-11; wording attested only from the undated current copy') and say so in the qualification. Add the definitional sentence ('By advanced artificial general intelligence, I mean AI systems that rival or surpass the human brain in complexity and speed') as the supporting quote for the sense; reword statement to 'for AI systems that rival or surpass the human brain in complexity and speed'.

items.findings: Quote verbatim in the cached post (paragraph 'The fairly undramatic story'); byline 'August 28th, 2011' present. 'Suggested' fairly renders 'came up with' in reply to his emailed request; '2002 or so' kept. Attribution kept as Goertzel's statement; qualification correctly separates title suggestion from earliest use. Post's own disclaimer ('I didn't actually coin the phrase') is consistent.

Quote verbatim. Goertzel writes that Gubrud 'had used the term in a 1997 article'; 'the term' in context is 'Artificial General Intelligence' (the book-title phrase just discussed). The statement says Gubrud 'had used the term 'AGI'', which, shown alone, implies the abbreviation; Gubrud's paper uses the full phrase, not 'AGI'. Identification of the article as the Foresight paper is the pack's inference and is properly flagged.
items.proposedFix: Reword: 'Mark Gubrud had used the term (in context, "Artificial General Intelligence") in a 1997 article on the future of technology and associated risks...'. Optionally add that the article is not named in the post.

Page images read (facsimile PDF pp. 1-2): title page and date August 31, 1955 confirmed; opening sentence 'We propose that a 2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence be carried out during the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College' confirmed. The second paraphrase misdescribes structure: 'the artificial intelligence problem' is in a separate line after the paragraph ('The following are some aspects of the artificial intelligence problem:'), not the end of the first paragraph. Substance fine. Note: this facsimile is an annotated copy with handwritten marginalia (from PDF p. 3), which the source version should mention.
items.proposedFix: Paraphrase: 'The opening paragraph proposes a 2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence...; the next line introduces the list as "some aspects of the artificial intelligence problem".' Note in the source version that the facsimile carries handwritten annotations.

items.findings: Page image (PDF p. 3, printed -2-) confirms the heading '3. Neuron Nets' and the paraphrase. But the earliest-located role is refuted by a quick index search, by the same title-as-indexed standard the pack itself uses for Campaigne 1959 and Burgin 1973: Crossref titles with listed names before 1955 include W. Pitts, 'The linear theory of neuron networks: The static problem', Bull. Math. Biophys. (1942-12, doi 10.1007/bf02478112); H. D. Landahl, 'A note on neural nets' (1944-06, doi 10.1007/bf02478485); Landahl and Runge, 'Outline of a matrix calculus for neural nets' (1946-06); D. Studley, 'Algebra of neural nets', Mathematics Magazine 22(3) (1949, doi 10.2307/3029684; reviewed by Church in JSL); Rapoport, 'Contribution to the probabilistic theory of neural nets' I-IV (1950). These are formal/mathematical models of nets of neurons (model of computation), which meets the criterion's 'natural or artificial ... model of computation, memory or learning'; the physiological-description exclusion does not obviously apply to Studley's algebra or the matrix calculus. The record's own qualification concedes the name 'was not new to the field'.
items.proposedFix: Remove the earliest-located-term role from this record (keep as 'use'). Open a correction on th-fam-connectionism: earliest located becomes Pitts 1942 ('neuron networks', a close variant; check whether the criterion accepts it) or Landahl 1944 ('neural nets'), pending reading of at least the abstract/first page; add these to the search block and gaps. If the criterion is meant to exclude mathematical biophysics, say so explicitly in the criterion.

items.findings: Preface (PDF p. 3, p. ii) read from image; cover confirms Report No. 85-460-1, January 1957. Paraphrase mostly faithful, but the statement fuses two things: the preface says the work was supported by CAL's internal research program, and that the concepts originated in the author's independent research in physiological psychology aimed at a brain analogue; 'The perceptron concept is a recent product of this research program' is ambiguous between the two. Statement and literal attribute the brain-analogue aim to the CAL internal program.
items.proposedFix: Statement: '...says the work was supported by the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory's internal research program, that its concepts originated in the author's research in physiological psychology aimed at a brain analogue, that the perceptron concept is "a recent product of this research program", and that the current effort aims at establishing the perceptron's technical and economic feasibility.' Adjust the object literal accordingly.

Crossref record verified (Machine Learning 20(3), 273-297, 1995-09). The earliest-located role is inconsistent with the family's own criterion and terms: th-fam-statistical-learning lists 'optimal margin classifier' and 'learnable' and admits 'a formal account of what can be learned from examples drawn from a distribution'. The pack itself holds Valiant (CACM, 1984-11; th-stat-valiant-1984-def) under this family, and Burges credits Boser, Guyon and Vapnik (1992), whose title names 'optimal margin classifiers'. Either is earlier than 1995. Quick Crossref check 'support vector' to 1995-09-30 found only Cortes-Vapnik and two Kulikov 1995 'support-vector algorithm' items (other sense on their face, optimisation).
items.proposedFix: Either (a) narrow the role to the name 'support-vector' (term-level record, not family naming) and say so, or (b) move the family's earliest located to Valiant 1984 ('learnable', formal account) or Boser et al. 1992 (title, as cited/indexed) with a correction entry. Also make the record's register clear that the text was not read.
